core_obligations: Reduce dominance to the generic point: by the same-chapter characterization of dominance through generic points of irreducible components, dominance is equivalent to mapping the generic point of X to the generic point of Y (proof lines 1644-1645).

Translate to ring maps on affine charts: for nonempty affine opens U and V with the image of U in V, the coordinate rings are integral domains and the generic points correspond to the zero ideals, so the previous condition is equivalent to injectivity of the ring map, which gives the equivalence of conditions (2), (3) and (4) at once (proof lines 1646-1656).

Repeat for local rings: for a point x with image y the local rings are domains and their zero ideals correspond to the generic points of X and Y, so the same argument shows that (2), (5) and (6) are equivalent, completing the cycle (proof lines 1658-1666).
proof_roadmap: Convert dominance into a statement about generic points (proof lines 1644-1645).

Read that statement off as injectivity of the coordinate ring map on some and hence every pair of affine charts, and equally off the local ring maps at some and hence every point (proof lines 1646-1666).
difficulty_reason: The lemma collects six equivalent conditions for a morphism of integral schemes to be dominant: dominance, hitting the generic point, injectivity of the coordinate ring map for some, respectively all, pairs of nonempty affine charts, and injectivity of the local ring map at some, respectively all, points (statement lines 1624-1642). The counted proof reduces the whole cycle to one observation made twice: on an integral scheme the generic point corresponds to the zero ideal, so dominance becomes injectivity of the ring map, and the same reading of the zero ideal works for local rings because the spectrum of a local ring corresponds to the points specializing to the given point (proof lines 1644-1666). It is H2: the proof is a clean reduction carried out in the counted span, with no independent research-level content.
